newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WTO chief to name judges in EU-US Cuba trade row.
newsitem.headline: WTO chief to name judges in EU-US Cuba trade row.

text.p: The European Union and the United States move into a major face-off on Thursday when World Trade Organisation chief Renato Ruggiero names members of a panel to look into the big powers' row over Cuba.

Although on the surface the issue is a trade dispute, diplomats said on Wednesday its underlying political dimensions could seriously sour relations between Brussels and Washington -- and damage the WTO -- despite soothing talk from both sides.

"There is a lot of concern that this could blow up in everyone's faces," said one envoy from a country which agrees with the EU complaint that the U.S. Helms-Burton law violates the WTO's open trading rules.
"Practically all (WTO) members support the Europeans on this, but many of us wonder if they are wise to press ahead," said another experienced trade negotiator.

EU officials said they expected WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero would name the three members of the panel on Thursday as he is obliged to under the partly U.S.-designed dispute settlement rules of the two-year-old organisation.
"The ball is in his court," said one.

Ruggiero, himself a one-time senior functionary in Brussels, has left little doubt that he would have preferred the two to find an accomodation on the row without bringing it to the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB).

Helms-Burton, signed into law a year ago by President Bill Clinton after Cuba shot down two planes from an exile group which had been flying anti-communist leaflet-dropping sorties over Havana, aims to limit foreign investment in the island.

It allows for U.S. citizens, including Cubans who fled after Castro's 1959 revolution, to bring cases in U.S. courts against foreign companies "trafficking", or investing in, property confiscated by his communist government.

Although Clinton has twice suspended for six months this aspect of the law, another clause under which executives of non-U.S. firms dealing with Cuba can be refused U.S. visas, has been applied -- to Europeans, Mexicans and Canadians.

In its complaint filed last October, Brussels argues the law amounts to "extra-territorial application of the U.S. embargo on trade with Cuba" and violates several articles of the WTO's underlying agreements on goods and service trade.
The United States has countered that the law is a national security issue, and therefore is outside the competence of the WTO, indicating it might refuse all cooperation with a panel.

U.S. officials have openly warned that if the dispute goes through the dispute settlement process and the panel finds against Washington, this would give fresh ammunition to U.S. politicians who oppose free trade accords and say membership of the WTO is a threat to national sovereignty.

The two sides have been involved in tortuous discussions for months to find a way out, but EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said at the weekend Washington was a long way from meeting European concerns.

After talks in Brussels with European Commission President Jacques Santer on Tuesday, new U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said she believed there were ways to resolve the issue "in an amicable fashion in the coming months".

But Brittan has left no doubt Washington will have to move substantially in the EU direction -- and agree to action on another U.S. law aimed at foreign firms investing in the Libyan and Iranian oil industries.
The panel will formally have six months to come up with its findings, but at any point the EU, if it feels progress is being made, can slow down or even halt proceedings.
But even if the panel reaches a decision, this can be appealed to the WTO's Appellate Body -- which would delay a final ruling for at least two, and possibly three, more months.
